title: What a taluqdar thought
body: During the revolt of 1857, Hanwant Singh, the Raja of Kalakankar near Rae Bareli, gave shelter to a British officer and conveyed him to safety. While taking leave of the officer, he is reported to have said: "Sahib, your countrymen came into this country and drove out our King. You sent your officers round the districts to examine the titles to the estates. At one blow you took from me lands which from time immemorial had been in my family. I submitted. Suddenly misfortune fell upon you. The people of the land rose against you. You came to me whom you had despoiled. I have saved you. But now - now I march at the head of my retainers to Lucknow to try and drive you from the country."

title: The Azamgarh Proclamation, 25 August 1857
body: The Azamgarh Proclamation is one of the main sources of our knowledge about what the rebels wanted. Issued in the name of the Badshahi (imperial) government, it addressed different social groups in separate sections. It accused the British of imposing exorbitant revenue demands on zemindars and auctioning their estates for arrears. It said the British had monopolised the trade in valuable goods such as indigo and cloth, leaving only trifles to native merchants, and taxed their profits with postages and tolls. It complained that natives in the civil and military services had little respect, low pay and no influence, while all posts of dignity went to Englishmen. It said English goods had thrown weavers, carpenters, blacksmiths and shoemakers out of employment. Finally, it called on pundits and fakirs, as guardians of the Hindu and Muslim religions, to join the war against the English. In each case it promised that the Badshahi government would remove these grievances.

title: Villagers as rebels
body: An officer reporting from rural Awadh (spelt Oude) during the British reconquest noted: "The Oude people are gradually pressing down on the line of communication from the North ... the Oude people are villagers ... these villagers are nearly intangible to Europeans melting away before them and collecting again. The Civil Authorities report these villagers to amount to a very large number of men, with a number of guns." Another British official, Forsyth, estimated that three-fourths of the adult male population of Awadh was in rebellion, and the region was brought under control only in March 1858 after protracted fighting.
